analysis.one_liner: Lets employers create employee committees to discuss working conditions without violating labor law.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 53-46 on July 10, 1996, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so employers could set up, fund, and participate in committees where employees discuss working conditions, quality, and productivity without that counting as an unfair labor practice. Under current law, employer-run committees that deal with workplace issues are treated as illegal 'company unions.' Supporters said this protects genuine workplace teamwork programs; opponents, including nearly all Senate Democrats and labor unions, said it legalizes employer-controlled bodies that can stand in for real collective bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who run employee involvement programs would be the main winners: they could establish and participate in employee committees without National Labor Relations Board liability. Workers on those committees would get a formal channel to raise issues like quality, scheduling, and productivity directly with management.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act so that it would not be an unfair labor practice for an employer to establish, assist, maintain, or participate in an employee organization addressing matters of mutual interest, including quality, productivity, and efficiency. [S2][S3]
Such committees could discuss terms and conditions of employment, as long as they do not negotiate or amend collective bargaining agreements. [S2][S3]

The bill's own findings say employee involvement structures operate in over 80 percent of the largest U.S. employers and an estimated 30,000 workplaces, so the exemption would cover a very large share of the workforce. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions and workers who rely on collective bargaining would bear the cost. Employer-controlled committees that address terms and conditions of employment could substitute for union representation, and any worker input through them would carry no enforceable agreement, since the committees are barred from negotiating contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill would legalize employer-dominated committees dealing with working conditions; its own findings acknowledge that employers in the 1930s used sham 'company unions' to avoid unionization, and opponents argued this exemption invites a modern version. [S3][S5]

Committees created under the bill could not negotiate or amend collective bargaining agreements, so employees could raise concerns through them but would have no power to bind the employer to any outcome. [S2][S3]
Minority views were filed when the committee reported the bill, and the final Senate vote split almost entirely along party lines, 53-46. [S5][S6]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated benefit — giving employees a structured voice in workplace decisions — is genuine, but the mechanism is entirely employer-controlled and produces no enforceable commitments. The practical effect is to make it easier for employers to address workplace issues through management-run committees rather than through independent union representation with a contract behind it. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill's value to employers comes from exactly what its critics fear: the committees lack bargaining power.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill on July 10, 1996, by tucking it into an unrelated House bill and passing that 53-46, mostly along party lines, but the House never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee held hearings in 1995 and 1996 and reported the bill favorably without amendment on May 1, 1996, placing it on the Senate calendar; minority views were filed. [S5]

On July 10, 1996, the Senate incorporated the measure into H.R. 743 as an amendment and passed H.R. 743 in lieu of S. 295 by a 53-46 roll call vote, with 51 of 53 Republicans voting yes and 45 of 47 Democrats voting no. [S5][S6]'
The bill was returned to the Senate calendar, and the House never passed the measure; it received no vote in the House before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997. [S1][S5]'

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The labor unions and Senate Democrats who opposed the bill came out ahead: workers' right to organize free of employer-run committees was left intact, and employers did not get the exemption from unfair labor practice liability.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired its hearings, reported it favorably from committee, and managed its consideration on the Senate floor, incorporating it into H.R. 743.

for.role: Senate Republicans voting on final passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes to pass the measure via H.R. 743, 53-46.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction alongside Senator Kassebaum.

against.role: Senate Democrats voting on final passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; committee Democrats filed minority views when the bill was reported.

against.name: Labor unions (AFL-CIO)
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing it would legalize employer-dominated committees that undercut independent union representation.

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split almost entirely by party: 51 of 53 Republicans voted yes while 45 of 47 Democrats voted no, with only 2 Democrats crossing over.

industries.industry: Large employers (corporations running employee involvement programs)
industries.note: The bill would free employers from National Labor Relations Board liability for employer-run employee committees covering quality, productivity, and working conditions. Its value to employers lies in addressing workplace issues through management-controlled bodies rather than through independent unions with bargaining power — a cost borne by workers' collective bargaining rights.

Employer-dominated committees that can discuss terms and conditions of employment could substitute for union representation and reduce workers' incentives to organize. Unions opposed the bill, and their interest ran alongside workers' right to bargain enforceable contracts.
